title: Urgent vs Non-Urgent Priority Task Queue
problemStatement: Implement `createPriorityScheduler()` that queues tasks labeled `'urgent'` (Priority 1) and `'transition'` (Priority 2). `flush()` must ALWAYS execute all urgent tasks before executing any transition tasks.
interviewTrap: In React 18's Lane model, urgent events (keystrokes) interrupt running transition fibers, discarding in-progress work to preserve 60fps input responsiveness.

testCases.name: Executes urgent tasks before older transition tasks
testCases.testFn: const s = createPriorityScheduler(); s.schedule(() => 'transition-1', 'transition'); s.schedule(() => 'urgent-1', 'urgent'); return s.flush();

testCases.name: Maintains FIFO order within same priority level
testCases.input: multiple urgent tasks execute in insertion order
testCases.testFn: const s = createPriorityScheduler(); s.schedule(() => 'u1', 'urgent'); s.schedule(() => 't1', 'transition'); s.schedule(() => 'u2', 'urgent'); return s.flush();

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React categorizes updates into Urgent (typing in an `<input>`, clicks) and Non-Urgent / Transition (filtering a 10,000 item list). Wrapping an update in `startTransition(() => setQuery(text))` allows React to interrupt the list render if the user types another keystroke.
stepByStepWalkthrough: 1. Render Phase: Fiber node evaluation and hooks linked-list dispatch for Lanes / Priority-Based Task Scheduling.
2. Reconciliation: Double buffering and fiber diffing mechanics.
3. Commit Phase: Synchronous/passive effect execution and DOM mutation.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In React Fiber, Lanes / Priority-Based Task Scheduling maintains state across work-in-progress trees and lanes scheduling priority.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does React Lanes scheduling resolve priority conflicts between urgent and transition work?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: React represents update priority using a 31-bit bitmask (`Lanes`). When an urgent update (`SyncLane`) arrives while a low-priority transition (`TransitionLane`) is rendering, React detects that `wipLanes` has lower priority than the pending lane. It immediately halts the transition work loop, saves the incomplete work, switches context to `SyncLane`, renders and commits the urgent update to the screen, and then resumes or restarts the transition work.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The pinnacle React 18 scheduler internals question.

realWorldUseCases.description: Keystrokes in an input field preempting 3D WebGL scene rendering updates.

howToExplain.opening: React Lanes use 31-bit integer bitmasks to represent task priority, allowing urgent tasks to preempt, suspend, and resume transition work.
keyPoints: Lanes replace legacy expiration times with composable bitmasks.
High-priority updates commit immediately without waiting for background work.
Background work resumes automatically once the main thread is clear.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Bitwise lane scheduling gives React the preemptive prioritization capabilities of a real-time operating system.
analogies: An air traffic control tower: a commercial airliner on final approach (transition) is told to circle the runway if an emergency medevac flight (urgent) needs to land immediately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming low-priority work can be starved indefinitely.
commonMistakes.why: React assigns expiration timestamps to all lanes. If a transition is preempted too many times, it expires and is upgraded to SyncLane, forcing it to commit.
commonMistakes.correct: Explain that lane expiration prevents transition starvation.

followUpDeepDive.question: What is getHighestPriorityLane in React reconciler source?
followUpDeepDive.answer: It uses bitwise math: `lane & -lane` (extracts the lowest set bit) to determine the highest priority lane in O(1) CPU operations.
